verdicts.correction: ARMeshGeometry.normals is per vertex, not per face: normals.count equals vertices.count (normals[i] belongs to vertices[i]), even though Apple's doc abstract says 'for each face'. Face normals must be computed from the three vertex positions (cross product), or by averaging the three vertex normals. The rest of the claim holds: classification is the per-face buffer (one UInt8 per face, 0 = .none), faces are triangles in ARGeometryElement, delegate callbacks and resetSceneReconstruction are as stated.
verdicts.reasoning: Apple's doc JSON for ARMeshGeometry/normals (iOS 13.4+) gives the abstract 'Rays that define which direction is outside for each face.' Real-world use contradicts this. A developer blog on LiDAR data in ARKit 3.5 (saboit.de, found by search but blocked for direct fetch) reports that the number of normals equals the number of vertices, not faces, and says this does not match the documentation. Search results also cite the ARKit SDK header comment for normals as 'Normal of each vertex in the mesh.' The MetalScanDemo Renderer.swift, a working Metal LiDAR renderer I fetched, binds meshGeometry.normals.buffer as vertex buffer index 1 next to vertices.buffer at index 0 for an indexed draw over faces. That only works if normals are indexed per vertex. Code that reads normals by face index would read the wrong data, or read past the end of the buffer, because faces usually outnumber vertices. The other sub-claims (sceneReconstruction .meshWithClassification with a supportsSceneReconstruction check, ARMeshAnchor via didAdd/didUpdate/didRemove, a per-face UInt8 classification buffer, resetSceneReconstruction, meshes flattened on detected planes) agree with Apple's sample 'Visualizing and interacting with a reconstructed scene' and common community code. I found no reports that these are broken on iOS 17 or 18.

verdicts.claim: Published iPhone LiDAR accuracy: small objects (>10 cm) ±1 cm absolute (Luetzenburg et al., Sci. Rep. 2021, iPhone 12 Pro); point-cloud RMSE vs known shapes 2.05 cm (iPhone 12 Pro) and 2.06 cm (iPhone 15) (Remote Sensing Letters 2026, tandfonline 10.1080/2150704X.2026.2720055); ARKit depth vs Faro ground truth agrees to 3.7 cm median (ARKitScenes analysis, rerun.io); reasonable accuracy up to about 4 m, noisy toward the ~5 m limit; building-scale scans with consumer apps put 69-83% of points within 5 cm of a terrestrial laser scan (iPhone 13 Pro, MDPI 2023); errors grow with distance and with path length because of SLAM drift.
verdicts.correction: Two sub-parts are wrong or overstated. (1) Remote Sensing Letters 2026 (Erland and Gaulton, vol 17 issue 12, pp 1620-1631, doi 10.1080/2150704X.2026.2720055) compared the iPhone 12 Pro Max and the iPhone 15 Pro, not the 'iPhone 12 Pro' and 'iPhone 15'. The base iPhone 15 has no LiDAR. The RMSE figures (2.05 cm and 2.06 cm) are for small primitive shapes (0.8 to 42.5 cm) scanned at 0.01 to 3.00 m, so they are close-range object figures, not room-scale figures. (2) The MDPI Geomatics 2023 paper (Askar and Sternberg, Geomatics 3(4):563-579) scanned a single laboratory room with four apps on an iPhone 13 Pro, not a building-scale scan. Abstract-level summaries report PolyCam standard deviation about 7 cm, a Scaniverse mean deviation of 44 cm, achievable accuracy of about 10 to 20 cm, and that no app met U.S. Institute of Building Documentation accuracy levels. The '69-83% of points within 5 cm' figure could not be confirmed and should be treated as unverified. Reword it as: 'room-scale scans with consumer apps on an iPhone 13 Pro deviated from TLS by several cm to decimetres depending on the app (std about 7 cm at best); app tracking dominates the error.' The Luetzenburg +/-1 cm for objects over 10 cm (plus +/-10 cm at 130 m cliff scale) and the rerun.io 3.7 cm median ARKit vs Faro figures are confirmed.
verdicts.reasoning: Direct fetches of nature.com, mdpi.com, rerun.io, tandfonline.com, zenodo.org and doaj.org were all blocked by the egress proxy (403/EGRESS_BLOCKED), so I checked the primary-source abstracts and metadata through search result snippets. Luetzenburg et al., Sci Rep 11:22221 (2021): 'accurate high-resolution models of small objects with a side length > 10 cm with an absolute accuracy of +/- 1 cm', and a 130 x 15 x 10 m coastal cliff at +/- 10 cm. Confirmed. Rerun blog 'Spotlight: Better labels for 3D reconstruction' (rerun.io/blog/arkitscenes-slam): 'Where the laser does have returns the ARKit depth and Faro laser scanner data agree to 3.7 cm median.' Confirmed. Remote Sensing Letters 2026: the RMSE values 2.06 cm and 2.05 cm are confirmed, but the Zenodo dataset record says 93 scans, 40 each from the iPhone 12 Pro Max and iPhone 15 Pro and 13 from a GeoSlam Zeb Horizon. The objects were 15 shapes of 0.8 to 42.5 cm at 0.01 to 3.00 m. So the claim names the models wrongly, and 'iPhone 15' is impossible because the base model has no LiDAR. MDPI Geomatics 2023 (2673-7418/3/4/30): the abstract describes 'a room occupied by laboratory inventory' scanned with 3D Scanner App, PolyCam, SiteScape and Scaniverse and compared with TLS. The reported figures are PolyCam std 7 cm, Scaniverse mean deviation 44 cm, and achievable accuracies of about 10 to 20 cm. 'Building-scale' overstates the scope, and I could not find the 69-83%-within-5-cm figure in any accessible abstract text. The general statements about range (about 4 to 5 m) and drift are qualitative and not contradicted, but none of the cited sources pins them down precisely.

verdicts.correction: The Remote Sensing Letters 2026 study (10.1080/2150704X.2026.2720055) compared an iPhone 12 Pro (Max) with an iPhone 15 Pro, not an iPhone 15; the base iPhone 15 has no LiDAR. Read it as: RMSE 2.05 cm (iPhone 12 Pro) vs 2.06 cm (iPhone 15 Pro), measured on fifteen small objects (0.8 to 42.5 cm) at 0.01 to 3.00 m, not on room-scale scans. The same study reports that the 15 Pro loses accuracy by 3 m and the 12 Pro struggles with small objects up close, so 'reasonable up to about 4 m' is optimistic for the newer IMX591 sensor. The '69-83% of points within 5 cm' figure for the iPhone 13 Pro Geomatics 2023 paper could not be confirmed. Available summaries say only that deviations were concentrated within 5 cm; treat the percentages as unverified. The other figures check out: Luetzenburg 2021 gives +/-1 cm for objects with sides over 10 cm and +/-10 cm for a 130 m cliff, and rerun.io reports a 3.7 cm median agreement between ARKit depth and the Faro scans.

(1) Luetzenburg et al. Sci Rep 2021: 'small objects with a side length > 10 cm with an absolute accuracy of +/- 1 cm' and a 130 x 15 x 10 m cliff at +/- 10 cm. Confirmed. The study 'compares the iPhone 12 Pro Max and iPhone 15 Pro' (Sony IMX591 vs IMX590) using fifteen objects of 0.8 to 42.5 cm at 0.01 to 3.00 m. It found 'minimal variation at 1 m', 'iPhone 12 Pro had greater issues scanning small close objects' and 'iPhone 15 Pro tended towards less accurate scans at the 3 m distance'. So the claim's 'iPhone 15' is wrong, since the non-Pro iPhone 15 has no LiDAR, and the RMSE is object-scale only. (3) rerun.io ARKitScenes blog: 'the ARKit depth and FARO laser scanner agree to 3.7 cm median' where the laser has returns. Confirmed. (4) Geomatics 2023 (mdpi 2673-7418/3/4/30), iPhone 13 Pro with four apps vs TLS: the abstract mentions a 'notable concentration of deviations ... within the 5 cm range', a 5 m range and software-dependent tracking issues. The specific 69-83% could not be verified. The drift and range statements match the qualitative findings.

open_question_answers.question: Does RoomCaptureSession's internally created (or user-supplied) ARSession run with sceneReconstruction = .meshWithClassification and frameSemantics containing .sceneDepth? Not documented. Verify on the first device build by logging `session.arSession.configuration` in captureSession(_:didStartWith:) and by counting ARMeshAnchors in the ARSessionDelegate. If it does not, the mesh coverage pass must run as a separate ARWorldTrackingConfiguration session (RoomPlan pass first, mesh pass second, or vice versa).
open_question_answers.answer: Evidence says no, not by default. Developer reports on Apple forums show the ARSession owned by RoomCaptureSession has frameSemantics without .sceneDepth (configuration?.frameSemantics.contains(.sceneDepth) == false), and a user who set sceneReconstruction = .mesh on captureSession.arSession found that RoomCaptureSession.run overrides it (no mesh shown). With a custom ARSession passed to RoomCaptureSession(arSession:) (iOS 17+), sceneDepth disappears from ARFrames once RoomPlan's run starts; the accepted workaround is to re-run the same ARSession with an ARWorldTrackingConfiguration that has sceneDepth (and add sceneReconstruction) after captureSession(_:didStartWith:) fires. WWDC23 says any custom ARSession with ARWorldTrackingConfiguration will be honored inside RoomCaptureSession. Configuration changes are applied asynchronously, so read session.arSession.configuration later (for example in didUpdate), not immediately. Architecture: design for a single shared ARSession created by the app, passed via init(arSession:), and re-configured with .meshWithClassification plus .sceneDepth in didStartWith; keep the two-pass fallback (separate ARWorldTrackingConfiguration mesh pass) behind a flag. Device test: start RoomCaptureSession(arSession: own), in didStartWith re-run ARWorldTrackingConfiguration with sceneReconstruction = .meshWithClassification and frameSemantics = [.sceneDepth, .smoothedSceneDepth optional]; after 5 s log configuration, frame.sceneDepth != nil, ARMeshAnchor count, and confirm RoomPlan still delivers didUpdate rooms and a final CapturedRoom with walls.

open_question_answers.question: Exact runtime semantics of completedEdges (observed vs geometrically closed) and how quickly an edge flips to completed; only community evidence exists. Measure on device.
open_question_answers.answer: Apple documents completedEdges only as 'An array of edges that outline the surface', with Edge cases top, bottom, left, right (iOS 16+). No official statement on whether it means observed or geometrically closed, or on timing. Best expectation from the naming and from the RoomCaptureView UI behaviour: an edge is listed once RoomPlan has confidently observed that boundary (for a wall, typically the floor and ceiling junctions and the corners with neighbouring walls). Architecture: treat completedEdges only as a soft coverage hint inside the live guidance, never as a gate for finishing a scan and never in the saved model. Device test: scan one wall slowly, log per didUpdate the wall identifier, timestamp and completedEdges; record time from first appearance to each edge, and whether edges ever drop out again; repeat with ceiling not scanned to see if top ever becomes completed.

open_question_answers.question: Can ARConfiguration.videoFormat be changed on the ARSession that RoomPlan drives without RoomPlan throwing invalidARConfiguration? Untested.
open_question_answers.answer: Undocumented; only a device test can settle it. Apple docs say invalidARConfiguration is thrown when the app attempts to set a value for arSession (the property), and WWDC23 says any custom ARSession with ARWorldTrackingConfiguration will be honored, highlighting high-quality image capture from ARKit with RoomPlan. That implies the app can pass its own session whose configuration has a chosen videoFormat, and captureHighResolutionFrame is usable. Forum evidence shows RoomPlan applies its own configuration at run, and re-running afterwards works for sceneDepth, so a videoFormat set before run is likely overwritten and must be re-applied after didStartWith. Architecture: do not depend on a non-default videoFormat during RoomPlan; use captureHighResolutionFrame for texture stills. Device test: in didStartWith re-run with videoFormat = ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.recommendedVideoFormatForHighResolutionFrameCapturing (and separately a 4K format from supportedVideoFormats), check didFailWithError, log configuration.videoFormat and frame.camera.imageResolution after 3 s, and confirm CapturedRoom is still produced.

open_question_answers.question: Real thermal timeline on an iPhone 13 Pro Max on iOS 18.3.2 with LiDAR + mesh overlay: minutes to .serious and .critical, and battery % per minute. No published numbers; collect from the session log.
open_question_answers.answer: No published numbers for this device and OS; only on-device logging settles it. Community developer reports describe LiDAR scanning plus Metal mesh rendering over 10 to 15 minutes driving phones into throttling and recommend stopping at .serious. Expectation for A15 in a room at about 22 C: .fair within a few minutes, .serious possible after roughly 10 to 20 minutes of continuous mesh plus RoomPlan plus overlay, .critical unlikely in normal room scans. Architecture: session log must record every ProcessInfo.thermalStateDidChangeNotification with elapsed seconds, and UIDevice battery level every 30 s; guidance should warn at .serious and auto-pause heavy work (overlay, texture capture) at .critical. Device test: full-brightness screen, start at 100 percent battery and .nominal, scan continuously for 30 min or until .critical, three runs, record times to each state and battery percent per minute.

open_question_answers.question: ARMeshAnchor update cadence and anchor block extent on iOS 18 (community says roughly 0.5-1 s and about 1-2 m blocks); affects only the hole-computation budget.
open_question_answers.answer: Apple documents only that mesh anchors constantly update and that updates are not intended to be real time; no cadence or block size is published. Community figures (updates around 0.5 to 1 s, blocks of roughly 1 to 2 m) are unverified. Architecture impact is small: compute holes incrementally per updated anchor identifier on a background queue with a throttle (for example at most every 0.5 s) so the budget holds for any cadence. Device test: in session(_:didUpdate:) log per ARMeshAnchor the identifier, timestamp and bounding box extent of its vertices; report median interval per anchor and median extent over a 2 minute room scan.

open_question_answers.question: Whether ARKit's confidenceMap on iOS 18 still uses raw values 0/1/2 with kCVPixelFormatType_OneComponent8 (Apple says read the format at runtime); assert it in a debug log on first run.
open_question_answers.answer: Apple doc for ARDepthData.confidenceMap (iOS 14+) says it holds an ARConfidenceLevel raw value per depth pixel and that the app should read the pixel format at runtime with CVPixelBufferGetPixelFormatType, giving kCVPixelFormatType_OneComponent8 as the example. ARConfidenceLevel has cases low, medium, high, which are Int raw values 0, 1, 2. Expect OneComponent8 with values 0 to 2 on iOS 18. Architecture: read the format at runtime, map bytes via ARConfidenceLevel(rawValue:), and fall back to treating all depth as medium if the format differs. Device test: on first frame log CVPixelBufferGetPixelFormatType of confidenceMap as a four-character code and a histogram of byte values; assert format L008 and max value 2.

open_question_answers.question: Whether Apple's 3.7 cm median ARKit-vs-Faro figure (ARKitScenes) is dominated by far-range pixels; if so the near-range depth term in the formula could be tightened after an on-device tape-measure calibration.
open_question_answers.answer: Could not fetch the ARKitScenes paper (arxiv.org is blocked here), so the 3.7 cm figure and its distance breakdown are not verified in this pass. Independent studies show Apple LiDAR error grows with range: iPad Pro LiDAR standard deviation about proportional to distance and rising sharply beyond about 4.5 m, and 1 to 2 cm accuracy at 1 to 3 m in iPhone studies. So a whole-frame median is likely inflated by far pixels, and a distance-dependent depth term (smaller near, larger far) is justified. Architecture: keep the depth error term as a function of range with parameters in one config struct, calibrated after a tape-measure protocol from TEST_PLAN.md. Device test: measure a flat wall at 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4 m with a tape; for each, log median and spread of sceneDepth (high confidence only) at the center patch versus tape distance.
